raw_record.support_text: The authors report 6 cases of granulomatous hepatitis in which a causal relationship with the intake of allopurinol was probable. The temporal relationship, the absence of other possible causes, and the characteristic pattern suggested that allopurinol was causative, and control biopsies in 2 cases showed disappearance of granulomas after discontinuation of allopurinol. Histology in all 6 cases showed granulomas (n=3) or granuloma-like reactions (n=3), with minimal to mild steatosis in most specimens, cholestasis in 1 case, and significant cholangitis in 1 case.
raw_record.extra_details: Granulomatous hepatitis in 6 patients. Histologically all cases showed granulomas (n=3) or granuloma-like reactions (n=3); epithelioid cells accompanied by lymphocytes, mixed with neutrophils or eosinophils; ill-defined granulomas/granuloma-like lesions with focal histiocyte/lymphocyte accumulations, ballooning, focal sometimes confluent necrosis and acidophilic degeneration. Minimal to mild steatosis in most specimens; cholestasis in 1 case; significant cholangitis in 1 case. Eosinophilic infiltration most prominent in cases with peripheral eosinophilia. None contained fibrin rings or fibrinoid material; 2 cases had vacuolated granulomas. Control biopsy in 2 cases showed disappearance of granulomas after allopurinol discontinuation; in one case a biopsy was done 17 days after discontinuation with no fibrin rings. Authors conclude fibrin-ring granulomas are uncommon in allopurinol-induced granulomatous hepatitis. Reference (5) cited as Vanderstigel et al.

reason: The 33-year-old carbimazole index case has dechallenge normalization and recurrent cholestatic hepatitis on a single-dose rechallenge. Reference [1] only supports background rare/fatal hepatitis; PubMed abstract confirms this patient is the reporting authors original case, not a cited case.

raw_record.support_text: A 33-year-old female with Graves' disease developed acute pancreatitis associated with mild cholestatic hepatitis and erythema nodosum one month into carbimazole therapy (45 mg daily), when she was already euthyroid. Carbimazole was interrupted and pancreatic and liver function normalized two weeks later. Rechallenge with a single dose of carbimazole led to a new episode of acute pancreatitis and cholestatic hepatitis one day later. The authors state that carbimazole should be added to the list of drugs capable of inducing these reactions and emphasize discontinuing the drug when pancreatic dysfunction appears.
raw_record.extra_details: Mild cholestatic hepatitis; rechallenge with a single dose of carbimazole reproduced pancreatitis and cholestatic hepatitis within one day. Liver tests showed slight AST/ALT rises with greater alkaline phosphatase (632 U/L, normal 80-270) and gamma-glutamyl-transferase (915 U/L, normal 0-50) increases and normal bilirubin; liver enlarged 3 cm. Liver function normalized two weeks after drug interruption. Concurrent acute pancreatitis and erythema nodosum were also attributed to carbimazole. Shortened interval between drug intake and symptom onset with repeated exposure and the hypersensitivity reactions point to an immune-mediated mechanism. Paper also notes (citing reference [1]) that severe, sometimes fatal hepatitis can rarely occur with carbimazole therapy, though less commonly than with methimazole.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective study in 149 neonates (5–182 days of age), intravenous paracetamol (initial dose of 20 mg/kg, then 10 mg/kg at intervals of 6, 8 or 12 hours depending on gestational age) was not associated with hepatotoxicity, with no changes in hepatic enzyme profiles during treatment and up to 2 days after the last dose. Similarly, a safety and pharmacokinetic study in 50 intensive-care neonates given multiple recommended intravenous paracetamol doses found no hepatotoxicity based on liver function tests (ALT, ALP and γ-glutamyl transferase).

raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective study (n=149 neonates, initial IV dose 20 mg/kg then 10 mg/kg every 6, 8 or 12 h for GA >36, 31–36 and <31 weeks respectively) showed no changes in hepatic enzyme profiles during treatment and up to 2 days after the last dose; safety/pharmacokinetic study (n=50 ICU neonates) showed no hepatotoxicity by ALT, ALP and γ-glutamyl transferase.
